apps.name: Shoji: your screen, for your eyes only
apps.tagline: Lock your Mac in a keystroke, come back with a touch.
apps.description:
## Shoji: your Mac, for your eyes only

  Shoji is a privacy screen for macOS. Press ⌘L and a soft screen slides over every display, keeping your work private while
  your Mac continues running exactly as before. Unlock with Touch ID or your Mac password and return to every window in the
  same place.

  Shoji is designed for the moments when you need privacy quickly:

  - Someone walks behind your desk.
  - You need to leave your Mac briefly.
  - You are working in a cafe, coworking space, classroom, or shared office.
  - You are presenting something and want to protect another app.
  - You are handing your Mac to someone without exposing private messages, email, notes, or files.
  - You want to keep a video, download, or long-running task active while hiding the screen.

  ### One shortcut to protect the whole Mac

  Press ⌘L to cover every display instantly. Shoji takes control of the keyboard while the screen is protected, so typing
  cannot accidentally reach your open applications.

  Unlock with Touch ID when available, or use your Mac password. Shoji verifies your password through macOS and never stores,
  logs, or sends it.

  Your windows do not move. Your apps do not quit. Your music keeps playing. Downloads and background work continue normally.

  If you stay away for longer than the time you choose, Shoji can hand off to the full macOS lock screen automatically.

  ### Five privacy modes

  Shoji gives you control over exactly what should be hidden.

  - Lock every display with Touch ID or your Mac password.
  - Blur the entire screen without requiring a password.
  - Blur one application while keeping the rest of the desktop visible.
  - Blur everything except the window you are currently using.
  - Lock only the application in front, useful when lending your Mac to someone or giving a demonstration.

  Each mode can use its own keyboard shortcut. You can also trigger lock and blur actions from screen corners or with shoji://
  links.

  ### Designed for real work

  Shoji is not intended to replace the macOS lock screen. The macOS lock is the heavy door you close when you are finished for
  the day. Shoji is the quick privacy layer you use throughout the day.

  It keeps your displays awake, leaves your windows exactly where you left them, and lets your Mac continue working behind the
  screen. When you need stronger protection, Shoji can hand over to the standard macOS lock screen.

  You can also:

  - Set separate blur and lock delays.
  - Leave a short note on the locked screen.
  - See the time and result of password attempts.
  - Lock or blur from a screen corner.
  - Customize every keyboard shortcut.
  - Use Shoji with multiple displays.
  - Keep new displays covered while Shoji is locked.
  - Use Increase Contrast and Reduce Motion accessibility settings.
  - Lock or blur using shoji://lock links.

  ### Privacy by design

  Shoji never captures your screen and never reads what is inside your windows. The blur is drawn by macOS itself, so Shoji
  does not need Screen Recording permission.

  Shoji does not require:

  - Screen Recording permission
  - Accessibility permission
  - Full Disk Access
  - An account or sign-in
  - Advertising identifiers
  - Analytics
  - Crash reporting

  Your screen stays on your Mac. Your passwords stay with macOS. Shoji only knows enough about window positions to place the
  privacy screen correctly.

  The app is signed and notarized by Apple. Update checks can be disabled, and they send no information about your files,
  screen, or Mac.

  ### Built for modern Intel and Apple silicon Macs

  Shoji runs on macOS 14 Sonoma or later and supports both Apple silicon and Intel Macs.

  The app is small, native, and designed to stay out of your way. It lives in the menu bar and is ready whenever you need to
  close the screen quickly.

  ### Try every feature free

  Every Shoji feature works for 24 hours from the first launch. After the trial, locking and blurring pause until you purchase
  a license. Anything already locked can still be unlocked, so you are never locked out of your own Mac.

  A Shoji license costs $14 once and works on up to three Macs. There is no subscription.

  Download Shoji and make your Mac private with one shortcut:

  https://everydaymactools.com/shoji/

apps.name: Now
apps.tagline: What you're listening to, with lyrics, on your desktop
apps.description:
Now puts what you are listening to on your desktop and keeps it there.

A small widget sits wherever you put it, showing the album art, the title, the artist, and how far through you are. Lyrics move with the music, line by line and word by word, so you can follow along without opening anything. Open the full-screen player and the cover fills the display against a background drawn from its own colours, leaning toward your pointer as you move it.

It follows whatever you already use. Apple Music, Spotify, TIDAL and Apple Podcasts as apps. YouTube Music, Spotify and Amazon Music in Safari or Chrome. Audio sent from an iPhone or iPad over AirPlay shows up the same way, cover art and progress included, whichever app it came from on the phone. Now switches between them on its own as you move from one to another, and films and TV are ignored, so a movie never turns up as a now playing.

The controls work everywhere the music does. Play, pause, skip, and scrub from the widget, the full-screen player or the menu bar. Drag across the cover to move through your music, and on Apple Music and YouTube Music the next cover slides in behind your finger before you let go. The back button restarts the current song first and steps back on a second press, the way it does everywhere else.

Four starting points, Elegant, Compact, Stacked, and Bold then move things around until it fits your desktop, with a live preview of every change as you make it. It can pause browser music while your microphone is in use, for calls or dictation, and resume once the mic is free. Desktop music apps are left alone, since they already handle that themselves.

Now is free, runs on Apple silicon, and needs macOS 14 or later. It asks for permission to talk to your music apps and nothing else. It never asks to record your screen or read your files, and nothing about what you play leaves your Mac. Updates are signed and install themselves, or you can turn that off.

Ascope is a native Mac app for App Store Optimization.

Add your own iPhone or Mac apps, or a competitor's, and Ascope checks where they rank for every keyword in 50+ App Store countries once a day, then keeps that history forever, so you can finally tell what your last metadata update really did.

## What you get

- **Daily rank tracking** across the top 200 App Store results in 50+ countries
- **Apple's own popularity score**, the same 5 to 100 scale Apple reports in Apple Search Ads. Estimates are marked with a ~ so you always know which is which
- **Keyword difficulty** from 0 to 100, based on the apps already ranking for the term
- **Keyword ideas** with popularity and difficulty already filled in, including searches where your app ranks in countries you don't track yet
- **Ratings per country**, with daily history and weekly change
- **Competitors**, including the apps Apple shows next to yours in You Might Also Like
- **An MCP server**, so Claude, Cursor or Claude Code can read your rankings and research keywords from chat

## Native, and small

A 4.5 MB download, universal for Apple silicon and Intel, signed with a Developer ID certificate and notarized by Apple. No Electron and no web wrapper. Your apps, keywords and ranking history stay on your Mac; the servers only see the search terms and app IDs needed for a lookup.

Requires macOS 14 Sonoma or later. Pro is $9.99 a month or $89.99 a year, with a full refund inside 14 days if it is not for you.

apps.name: Lofi Space
apps.tagline: A native macOS menu-bar app for lofi music with animated scenes, an ambient mixer, custom soundscapes, and one-tap focus.
apps.description:
Every focus setup I had ended the same way: a browser tab playing a lofi stream, buried under twenty other tabs, occasionally hijacked by an ad — and always the first thing to die when I quit the browser to clear my head. Music that's supposed to help you concentrate shouldn't need a tab, an account, or a monthly bill.

So I built the thing I actually wanted: **Lofi Space**, a native macOS lofi player that lives in your menu bar and gets out of the way.

## What it is

Lofi Space is a small, real Mac app — Swift and SwiftUI, not a web page in a wrapper. It sits in your menu bar as a single icon. Click it and a compact popover slides down with the track that's playing, transport controls, and volume. That's the whole surface area on most days. When you want more, a full-screen launcher opens the scene library.

Each **scene** is a room: an animated looping video paired with an original lofi mix written for it.

- **Zen Café** — vinyl spinning, espresso machine winding down.
- **Cozy Room** — desk lamp, soft jazz, rain on the windowsill.
- **Night Tokyo** — neon in puddles, the hum of late trains.
- **Forest Dawn** — birds waking up while the world is still gold.

Pick a room, hit play, stay a while. New scenes ship in free updates — never as a second purchase.

## Who it's for

People who work with music on for hours and don't want to think about it: developers, designers, writers, students, anyone who opens a laptop and needs the room to settle before the work starts.

If you already have Spotify and a favorite playlist, you may not need this. Lofi Space is for the people who kept a lofi stream open all day and quietly resented what it cost them — the tab, the ads, the account, the algorithm deciding what focus sounds like today.

## What makes it different

- **It's native.** Instant cold start, tiny footprint. Media keys work. Now Playing and Control Center work. Cover art shows in the menu bar. All the things a Mac app is supposed to do and a browser tab never quite does.
- **It works offline.** Audio is cached to disk against a budget you set, from 100 MB up to 5 GB. Scene videos are cached too, so the visuals keep looping with the Wi-Fi off. Pin a scene and its whole track list is locked to disk, safe from eviction. It works on the plane.
- **It respects the call.** Auto-pause watches for other apps using your speakers or mic and pauses playback — then picks up five seconds after the call ends. It needs *no microphone permission*: macOS exposes per-process audio activity as metadata, so the app never records, watches, or transmits anything.
- **It layers.** The ambient mixer adds six loops on top of the music — rain, fireplace, birds, waves, river, white noise — each with its own slider. Rain over a jazz mix at 55%, fireplace at 20%. Build the room you want.
- **It stays out of the way.** `⌥ + ⌘ + Space` to play or pause, `⌥ + ⌘ + →` to swap scenes, `⌥ + ⌘ + ↑↓` for volume — from any app, without ever looking at the window.

## The pricing, and why

Free is free forever. Not a trial, not a countdown, not three scenes and a paywall: the player, the menu bar popover, the launcher, every built-in scene with its full artwork, favorites, and cache control — all free, no account, no sign-up.

**Pro is $4.99. Once.** It adds the ambient mixer, auto-pause for calls, global hotkeys, and pinned offline downloads, plus every future scene and update. Buy it once and you own it. Purchases go through Polar with a 14-day refund window.

There's no subscription because a lofi player shouldn't have a subscription. There's no account because a music player doesn't need to know who you are. You register a license key once, online, and the app is yours offline after that.

## Why it matters

The small tools you touch every day set the temperature of your work. Most of them have gotten heavier — more accounts, more upsells, more notifications, more surface begging for attention. This one is deliberately the opposite: an app you set up in about a minute and then genuinely forget, doing exactly one thing well in the corner of your screen while you do the thing that actually matters.

Play, focus, forget it's there. That's the whole pitch.

**Requirements:** macOS 14 Sonoma or later. Universal binary — Apple Silicon and Intel are both first-class. Download at [lofispace.app](https://lofispace.app).

apps.name: ItsPaint
apps.tagline: Native Mac paint and markup. No account, no network.
apps.description:
Paintbrush, the macOS MS Paint clone, has not shipped since 2021 and is
Intel-only. Windows 11 Paint has meanwhile become a real editor — layers,
transparency, generative fill — but it wants a Microsoft account and, for the
interesting parts, a Copilot+ NPU. On macOS the only thing in the gap is Markup,
which cannot number the steps of a bug report or redact a token.

ItsPaint is a native AppKit paint and markup app for that gap. Twelve tools,
fifteen shapes, both colours and the palette visible at once, and no workspace to
set up before the first stroke.

**What it is for**

- Paste a screenshot, drop auto-numbered step badges on it, pixelate the API key,
  and send it — the two jobs Markup will not do.
- Instant Alpha and one-command background removal, which declines rather than
  guessing: if the flood would take essentially the whole canvas, nothing changes
  and it says so.
- Paste an image larger than the canvas and the canvas grows to hold it, so
  nothing is cropped when you place it.
- Rotate by any angle, with the canvas growing to fit the corners.
- Export to PNG, JPEG, TIFF, BMP, GIF, HEIC, AVIF, PDF and ICO.

**What is underneath**

Two layers: a UI-free drawing engine of 5,838 lines, and 8,251 lines of AppKit
and SwiftUI on top of it. Pixels are premultiplied RGBA8, every edit returns the
rectangle it changed, and the canvas redraws only that area. No third-party
dependencies at all.

Documents are a PNG with a JSON sidecar, so the artwork opens in anything, with
or without ItsPaint.

**No network, and it is checkable**

Neither `com.apple.security.network.client` nor `.server` is requested, so the
sandbox refuses a socket whatever the code asks for. `otool -L` on the shipped
binary finds no `CFNetwork`, no `Network.framework` and nothing outside the
system on either architecture. A grep of the source for the networking APIs
returns nothing. The three commands are in the README; the point is that you do
not have to take the claim on trust.

Free, MIT, notarised, macOS 14 or later. `brew install --cask joshlin2201/itspaint/itspaint`, or the disk image from GitHub Releases.

Public beta — the version number is honest about that.

apps.name: Snapdown
apps.tagline: Turn anything on your Mac screen into clean Markdown
apps.description:
## Capture the structure, not just the words.

Snapdown is a native macOS menu bar app that turns any selected area of your screen into clean, structured Markdown.

It was built for the moments when information is visible but not actually selectable, such as documentation, tables, error messages, slides, settings panels, reading excerpts, and text inside images.

Traditional OCR often recovers the words but loses what made the content useful. Headings become ordinary lines, lists collapse into paragraphs, tables lose their relationships, and reading order becomes difficult to follow. Snapdown preserves useful structure so the result is ready to paste into a note, document, issue, prompt, or Markdown file without rebuilding it first.

## How it works

1. Press the global keyboard shortcut.
2. Drag over any visible region of your Mac screen.
3. Snapdown turns the selection into structured Markdown.
4. The Markdown is copied to your clipboard and saved locally.
5. Paste it wherever you need it.

Snapdown keeps the capture loop small so you can collect what you need without interrupting your work.

Every capture is stored in your local history as an ordinary Markdown or text file, making it easy to find, edit, move, and reuse later.

## Many captures. One document.

Some content is too large or complex for one screenshot. Aggregate Mode lets you capture it in smaller, natural sections while building a single Markdown document.

Use it to combine several lecture slides, documentation sections, table fragments, reading excerpts, or parts of a long interface. Each new capture is appended to the same document, keeping related material together and reducing the noise that comes from capturing an entire screen at once.

## Built for real Mac workflows

Developers can move error messages, API documentation, tables, terminal output, and interface states into Cursor, Claude, GitHub, Linear, or project documentation.

Writers and product teams can turn rendered pages, comparison tables, settings screens, and UI content into editable material for specifications, release notes, and issues.

Students and researchers can capture lecture slides, course portals, formulas, tables, and reading excerpts into Obsidian, Notion, study notes, or an AI tutor.

Wherever Markdown goes, Snapdown gives screen content a useful way to follow.

## Private by design

Every capture is processed locally on Apple silicon.

Your screenshots are never uploaded. Your captured documents stay private on your Mac, and Snapdown continues working offline.

## Tips for better captures

* Capture smaller, natural sections instead of an entire screen. Aggregate Mode can combine those sections into one document while reducing visual noise.
* Zoom in before capturing dense text, tables, or formulas. Clearer source pixels give Snapdown more detail to work with.

**Anything on your screen. Now in Markdown.**

apps.name: Ply
apps.tagline: Your apps forget what you were thinking. Ply keeps it.
apps.description:
You're in the middle of something: a chat with your mom, a listing on Airbnb, a file in your code editor. A thought comes up. *Send her the flight times tonight. Ask about parking. Fix that spacing later.* You switch apps, and it's gone.

**Ply keeps the thought with the work.** It's a small companion for your Mac that remembers what you were thinking, right where you were thinking it.

## How it works

Press **⌥ ⇧ Space** in any app, website, or code folder and write a note, a task, or a reminder. Ply saves it to that exact place. The next time you open the same chat, page, or project, your notes are waiting for you.

There's nothing to set up and no link to paste. Ply notices where you are and keeps things together.

- **Notes** for the thoughts you don't want to lose
- **Tasks** you can check off when they're done
- **Reminders** that show up as Mac notifications at the time you pick
- **Saved pages and files**, with `@` mentions to point back at them later
- **Search** one project, or everything at once, with **⌘ F**

## Works where you already are

Messages, Gmail, Google Maps, Airbnb, Booking.com, YouTube, Figma, Cursor, Shopify, and pretty much any app or website you use. Each conversation keeps its own notes, so the notes about a friend's birthday stay in that chat. If Ply doesn't recognize an app, it still gets its own place.

## Talk to it with Ply Pro

Hold **⌥ A**, say it, and let go. Ply turns what you said into a note, a task, or a reminder for the place you're in. You can also ask it to:

1. Save the page or file you're on
2. Check something off, or undo it
3. Answer questions from the notes you've captured

Your voice is transcribed on your Mac.

## Private by design

- Everything you capture is saved **on your Mac**. Nothing syncs, and nothing is tracked.
- Ply reads window titles, page addresses, and file paths. It **never** reads the text on your screen or your messages.
- Apps you merely pass through aren't recorded. A place is only saved once you write something in it.
- Links that carry sign-in details are never saved, and tracking parameters are removed.
- Export everything as Markdown or JSON whenever you like.

## Pricing

- **Free:** the whole app for up to 5 places. No account needed.
- **Own it:** buy Ply once for unlimited places and every 1.x update. No subscription.
- **Ply Pro:** $4.99 a month with a 7-day free trial. Includes the full app plus talking to Ply. After 2 months of Pro, Ply is yours to keep, even if you cancel.

### Requirements

An Apple silicon Mac running macOS 14 or later. Ply for iOS is coming soon.

Download it free at [getply.app](https://getply.app).

apps.name: TOMA
apps.tagline: ⇧⌘4, but for video. Record a region as MP4, HEVC or GIF.
apps.description:
Toma is ⇧⌘4 for video. Press ⌥⇧⌘4, drag a rectangle, and it starts recording the moment you let go. Press the shortcut again to stop. There is no settings window, no account and no editor.

## Decide when you see it

When the recording ends, a thumbnail appears at the bottom right, just like a screenshot, with the clip playing on a loop. Pick the format there:

- **MP4**: H.264, plays everywhere.
- **HEVC**: half the size, ideal on Apple devices and modern browsers.
- **GIF**: no player needed, for READMEs, pull requests, chats and docs.

Drag the thumbnail into Slack or Mail, copy it to the clipboard, or do nothing and it saves in the format you used last.

## Light, for real

Toma re-encodes every clip for quality rather than a fixed size, so text stays sharp and a still screen weighs almost nothing: 4 seconds of scrolling text at 1120 × 720 comes out at 0.46 MB as MP4 and 0.25 MB as HEVC. The GIF encoder is built for screens and only stores what changes between frames.

## Small and private

- Records the Mac's sound and, if you want, your microphone.
- Works offline, with no analytics. Files stay in the folder you choose.
- Native Swift on ScreenCaptureKit, under 1 MB, signed and notarized by Apple.
- Free and open source under the MIT licence: [github.com/felipebasurto/toma](https://github.com/felipebasurto/toma)

Requires macOS 26 or later, on Apple silicon or Intel.

apps.name: defocus

apps.description:
defocus.me is a lightweight macOS utility that helps you concentrate by keeping the window you are working in sharp while softly fading everything else into the background.

Your desktop can quickly become crowded with multiple apps, documents, browser windows and notifications. defocus.me creates a calmer visual environment without changing your workflow. The active window remains clear and easy to follow, while inactive windows are gently blurred, darkened or both.

The effect follows your focus automatically. Switch from Safari to Xcode, from a document to your notes, or from one app to another, and defocus.me updates instantly to keep your current window in focus.

Choose your preferred focus style

Customize how your desktop looks with three visual modes:

- Blur — soften inactive windows while preserving their colours and overall atmosphere.
- Dim — darken inactive windows so the active app stands out clearly.
- Both — combine blur and dimming for a stronger focus effect.

You can adjust the blur and dim intensity to match your preferences, from a subtle reduction of distractions to a more pronounced focus layer.

Designed to stay out of your way

defocus.me lives quietly in the macOS menu bar and does not add another application window to your daily workflow. Toggle the effect whenever you need it using the global keyboard shortcut, or simply shake your cursor to turn focus on or off.

You can also configure defocus.me to:

- Launch automatically when you log in.
- Change the global keyboard shortcut.
- Toggle focus by shaking the cursor.
- Adjust cursor-shake sensitivity.
- Fade other windows belonging to the active application.
- Automatically turn off while using full-screen apps.
- Exclude specific applications from the effect.
- Keep the menu bar and Dock sharp at all times.

Private by design

defocus.me runs locally on your Mac. It does not require an account, does not record your screen, and does not collect analytics or usage data. Your screen content and window contents are never captured, uploaded or profiled.

The app uses macOS window information only to determine which window is currently active and where to apply the visual effect. Everything happens on your device.

Native, lightweight and built for Mac

defocus.me is a native macOS app designed to feel natural on modern Macs. The visual effect is handled by the macOS compositor, allowing the app to remain small, responsive and unobtrusive while you work.

Whether you are writing, coding, researching, editing, studying or managing several projects at once, defocus.me helps create a quieter desktop and gives your current task more room to breathe.

apps.description:
Discrity sits in your Mac's menu bar and tells you, in plain words, what is using your camera, microphone and speaker, and what used them before.

Usage history: every time an app turns on your camera, microphone or speaker, Discrity records which app, when, and for how long. Filter by device, app and day, see a daily chart, and check which addresses an app was connected to while it used your camera or mic. The history stays on your Mac.

See and stop: see which app is using each device right now and for how long. One button mutes the microphone and closes every app using the camera or mic, then tells you exactly what it stopped. You can also use a keyboard shortcut or a floating stop button.

Calm alerts: Discrity names the app within about two seconds. Apps you trust only change the menu bar icon. New apps get a short notice that hides itself. Apps it can't identify get a warning that stays until you respond.

Away watch: lock your Mac and walk away. When you return, Discrity reports any keyboard, mouse or trackpad use, MacBook lid opening, power cable or USB changes while you were gone.

Speaker guard: when headphones disconnect, the speakers are muted so nothing plays out loud by surprise.

Private by design: no account, no upload, no analytics. Discrity never records audio, video, screenshots or typed text. It goes online only to check your license and, when you ask, for updates.

Honest about limits: Discrity warns and stops apps after they start, not before, and it is not antivirus.

apps.tagline: Native macOS menu bar app for converting unix timestamps
apps.description:
UnixTime lives in your menu bar and makes working with Unix timestamps effortless. Just hover over the menu bar icon and a tooltip instantly shows what is currently on your clipboard, its matching counterpart (the corresponding timestamp or date), and exactly what a click would copy — all before you click anything. A single click then copies the converted result to your clipboard, ready to paste wherever you need it. If your clipboard is empty, a click copies the current timestamp in your chosen format instead.
 
Conversion works in both directions and is detected automatically: copy a timestamp to get a date, or copy a date to get a timestamp. Beyond the classic Unix seconds and milliseconds, UnixTime also handles microseconds, nanoseconds, and a range of platform-specific epoch formats used by .NET, Windows, Chrome/WebKit, Apple, Mozilla, and classic Mac systems, as well as the astronomical Julian Day Number. Each timestamp is shown together with its unit (s, ms, ns, and so on) so there is never any doubt about what you are looking at.
 
A built-in date and time calculator lets you build and adjust specific moments in time: enter a date, add or subtract seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months or years, switch between time zones, and generate random dates or times for testing. Every conversion is saved to a history list — including which app you copied the value from — so you can copy any previous result again with a single click.
 
You stay in full control of the interface. Show, hide, and reorder any format, set your preferred timestamp or date format as the default, and create as many custom date formats as you like, each with its own name and pattern. The app is fully localized in 12 languages, supports light and dark mode, and can start automatically at login. It is built natively with SwiftUI, so it stays fast, responsive, and light on system resources.
 
## Features:
- Converts Unix timestamps to dates and dates to timestamps, auto-detected from the clipboard
- Live tooltip preview: see the current clipboard value, its counterpart, and what a click will copy — before you click
- One click copies the conversion result straight to your clipboard, ready to paste
- Copies the current timestamp in your chosen format when the clipboard is empty
- Timestamp units: seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, nanoseconds
- Platform-specific formats: .NET Ticks, Windows FILETIME / LDAP, Chrome/WebKit, Cocoa/NSDate, HFS+ (classic Mac), Mozilla PRTime, Julian Day Number
- Exact sub-second precision (microseconds and nanoseconds) for the current time
- Unit label (s, ms, ns, …) shown next to every timestamp
- Many built-in date formats, plus unlimited custom date formats with your own names
- Date and time calculator with time zones, add and subtract, time presets, and random date/time generation
- History of recent conversions, including the source app you copied from
- Show, hide, and reorder formats; set any format as your default
- Localized in 12 languages
- Light and dark mode
- Launch at login
- Native SwiftUI app with a small footprint and instant response

## Who it's for:
UnixTime is made for anyone who runs into Unix timestamps as part of their daily work — primarily developers, but just as much for DevOps engineers, system and database administrators, QA and test engineers, data engineers and analysts, security researchers, and technical support staff. If you regularly see raw epoch numbers in logs, APIs, databases, config files, or datasets and need to know what they actually mean, UnixTime is built for you.
 
## Typical use cases:
- Figuring out what a timestamp in a log line or stack trace really means
- Converting epoch values from an API request or response
- Debugging token and session expiry, such as JWT iat and exp claims
- Reading and writing database timestamps stored as Unix seconds or milliseconds
- Decoding platform-specific values like Windows FILETIME, .NET Ticks, or Chrome/WebKit and Cocoa timestamps found in logs and forensic data
- Grabbing the current timestamp in a specific format to paste into code, a test, a query, or a config file
- Building a precise date and time as test data, and shifting it across time zones
- Generating random dates or times to test time-dependent behavior
- Quickly checking a date against its timestamp (and back) without leaving the app you are working in

VIDEO WALLPAPERS

COLOR GRADING

apps.name: Vibe in Color
apps.tagline: 200 original Codex themes, previewed and imported on Mac.
apps.description:
Vibe in Color is a free native macOS utility for people who spend a lot of time in the Codex app and want their workspace to feel a little more personal.

I originally built it for myself after discovering that “pick a theme and get back to work” was apparently not how this was going to go.

## What it does

Vibe in Color contains **200 original themes**, organised into 10 work vibes. Each vibe has 10 light and 10 dark themes, ranging from quiet, low-contrast palettes to considerably less quiet late-night colours.

You can:

- Browse themes by vibe or explore the complete collection
- Preview each theme against realistic chat, code and diff views
- Test themes with fonts already installed on your Mac
- Search the collection and save favourites
- Import your choice through Codex’s built-in theme importer

The previews are there because a colour palette can look lovely in isolation and become completely unusable the moment it meets a code diff.

## Why it exists

Colour affects how I read, focus and settle into longer coding sessions. Sometimes I want something calm and nearly invisible; sometimes the correct answer is called **Burning the Midnight Oil**.

Vibe in Color makes it easy to explore those moods without manually editing theme files or repeatedly importing themes just to discover that one comment colour is impossible to read.

## Privacy and requirements

- Completely free
- Apple-notarized
- No account
- No analytics
- No network access
- Built for Apple silicon
- Requires macOS 14 or later

It is a small utility I made for myself and decided to share with anyone else who might enjoy it.

apps.name: Secrets
apps.tagline: Secrets is a secure password manager for both macOS and iOS.
apps.description:
Secrets is an app for storing all of your passwords and anything else you want to keep … secret!

There are lots of things in our daily lives that we don’t want other people to know like credit card details, bank details, and of course, passwords. Secrets can protect all of those things and more in an app that’s easy to use but still secured by strong encryption and advanced sync technology.

Because we think that your secrets should be yours and yours alone, your passwords and information are never synced with our servers. If you choose to sync your information between devices it will be encrypted and securely saved in iCloud. Secrets uses strong 256-bit encryption and locks your information behind biometric (Face ID or Touch ID) and alphanumeric (a strong and unique passphrase) protection.

Despite that, Secrets is full of features that you’re going to love using and will make using your passwords and other information a breeze.

# Features

• Store all of your passwords, passkeys, credit cards, bank details, and other information so that it’s always there when you need it.
• Create new, secure, and private passwords for new apps and services. No more trying to come up with a unique password yourself.
• Generate one-time passcodes for apps and services that offer two-factor authentication.
• Get all of your passwords and information into Secrets with ease — import from 1Password, LastPass, and other popular services or import using a CSV file.
• Take your passwords with you. Secrets supports iCloud syncing so your information is always available and up-to-date.
• Access your passwords when you need them — Secrets for iPhone and iPad securely  integrates with browsers on Windows and Linux so your passwords are never more than a few taps away.
• Use password AutoFill to quickly enter usernames and passwords on your Apple devices.

# Privacy

We don't have access to your information, including usernames and passwords. Not even in encrypted form!
Synced information doesn’t use our servers and nothing leaves your device or iCloud (when syncing is enabled).
Information is stored using modern cryptographic algorithms and 256-bit encryption.
Use Touch ID or Face ID to unlock Secrets or set up a strong passphrase — or both! You can even use your Apple Watch to unlock Secrets on the Mac.
Automatic locking ensures that Secrets keeps all of your information locked away even if your phone/computer is stolen.

apps.name: ScreenPlace
apps.tagline: Effortlessly put every window in its place on your Mac.
apps.description:
ScreenPlace remembers exactly where every window should be on your Mac and automatically puts it back in its place. Never rearrange or resize a window again because ScreenPlace can handle it for you automatically.

Badge is the defining experience of ScreenPlace - a floating companion that stays close to your windows and lets you snap them back into place with a single click. You can also group your apps into separate workspaces and switch between them in seconds, save reusable templates for the window sizes and positions you frequently use, and have a separate layout for every display setup you use so the right one applies the moment you connect. Global shortcuts let you switch between workspaces or apply window sizes and positions from anywhere on your Mac, and with auto-apply, your windows are already in place by the time you need them.

ScreenPlace is built to stay out of the way and just work. It's a fully native macOS app, customizable down to the smallest detail, with a one-time payment and no subscription - so you can set it up once to suit how you actually work, and let it quietly keep all of the windows in place on your Mac.

## Key Features
**Badge** - a floating companion for every window you use that lets you snap it back into its place, as well as save the current size and position. It also hides automatically when both size and position already match.
**Unlimited workspaces** - group your windows by what you're working on and switch between workspaces right from the menu bar or using a keyboard shortcut.
**Multi-display support** - easily manage windows across all of your monitors with per-display configurations.
**Auto-apply** - ScreenPlace can automatically apply window sizes and positions when you launch your apps so there's nothing to rearrange or resize when an app opens.
**Global shortcuts** - switch between workspaces or apply window sizes and positions with keyboard shortcuts without even opening the app.
**Reusable templates** - set the exact size and position you want, save it as a template, and apply it to any window in just a few clicks.
**Smart window matching** - match windows by title, index, or pattern so the right window is always in its place.
**Endless customization** - tailor ScreenPlace down to the smallest detail so it suits the way you work.
**Up and running instantly** - grant accessibility access, add windows, and you're done.

## Pricing
You can use ScreenPlace completely for free, and there is an ultra version available that can be purchased as a one-time purchase.

After the first licence activation and an approximately 500 MB language-model download, recording and transcription run locally. If transcription fails, the recording remains in local History for another try. History is deleted automatically after seven days.

Dictaty requires macOS 14 or later. The first release supports Apple silicon Macs. Dictaty 1.0.1 (Build 37) is distributed as a DMG signed with the RELMOS AG Developer ID and notarized by Apple.

A limited launch allocation is free while places remain. Afterwards, one personal licence for one Mac costs €29 once, including applicable VAT. The licence does not expire and includes Dictaty 1.x updates. There is no account or subscription.

apps.name: Zush
apps.tagline: AI File Renamer & Organizer
apps.description:
Zush is an AI file renamer and organizer for Mac and Windows. It batch renames files based on what's actually inside them: drop in a messy folder of screenshots, PDFs, photos, videos, audio, or documents, and Zush reads the content of 100+ file formats to generate clean, consistent filenames.

Custom AI Blocks set Zush apart. Describe any detail in a short prompt — brand name, client, invoice number, case ID — and Zush extracts it from the file straight into the filename. Mix custom blocks with 145+ built-in naming blocks (dates, camera metadata, finance, legal, travel) in reusable templates.

Privacy comes first: run Zush 100% offline with local Ollama models, so files never leave the device. Or bring your own API key (BYOK) and choose the provider you trust — Gemini, OpenAI, Claude, or Groq. No forced cloud, no lock-in. Offline AI and BYOK are available in PRO version.

Zush also watches folders and renames new files as they arrive, adds smart metadata and tags for instant search, and keeps a full rename history with one-click undo. Free to start, no signup, no credit card.

apps.name: CamCue
apps.tagline: AI interview and meeting assistant for Mac
apps.description:
CamCue is an AI interview and meeting assistant for Mac. It drafts answers to spoken and on-screen questions using your CV, a job description, documents, and custom instructions.

Listen recognizes questions from computer and microphone audio. Capture analyzes the whole screen; Select reads the area you choose. Use Interview, Coding Interview, Quiz/Test, or Call mode, save context presets, and practice with the built-in Listen demo. Local session history keeps questions and answers available for review. Focus Mode gives you a compact, movable window with adjustable transparency.

Speech recognition runs locally. Raw Listen audio is not uploaded or saved, while recognized text and relevant context are sent for AI processing. An internet connection and a CamCue account are required. No personal API key is needed. Stealth requests capture exclusion where supported; check the receiving view before screen sharing.

Start free with limited AI credits. PRO includes unlimited AI credits for Listen, Capture, and Select: US$9 every 3 days, US$19 every week, or US$69 every month. Plans renew until canceled. Technical rate and session limits apply; checkout shows final prices and taxes.

Requires Apple Silicon M1 or later and macOS 14.2 or later. CamCue is also available for Windows x64. Support: support@camcue.app.

apps.name: Keelhaven
apps.tagline: Privacy-first macOS menu-bar backup app powered by restic.
apps.description:
Privacy-first Mac backup to your own storage. Free and open source (GPLv3) — no subscription, no telemetry.

Keelhaven wraps the battle-tested restic engine in a native SwiftUI menu bar app: pick folders, pick a destination you own (external drive, any S3-compatible bucket, or SFTP/NAS), set a schedule — your files are encrypted on your Mac before they leave it.

The engine, wizard, scheduled backups, whole-snapshot restore, periodic repository verification, and retention presets all work — app and website in English and Simplified Chinese; file-level browsing inside snapshots is next.

apps.name: Unfumble

apps.description:
If you type in more than one language, you know the dance: start a sentence, realize the keyboard was on the wrong layout, delete the gibberish, switch languages, retype. Dozens of times a day.

Unfumble was built to kill that dance. It's an automatic keyboard language switcher for Mac - it detects the language you're writing and switches for you, as you type. And when a word does land in the wrong layout, it's rewritten the moment Unfumble recognizes what you meant.

It's for anyone who lives in two (or more) languages - Hebrew, Arabic, Russian, Ukrainian, Greek, Thai, and English today. It learns which language you use in each app and website, so your keyboard is already right before you type.

Why it matters:

Switching layouts by hand is a chore the OS never solved - the globe key is basically a manual gear shift. Unfumble makes it automatic.
It's 100% on-device. Keystrokes are inspected only to fix the current word - no telemetry, nothing leaves your Mac. Notarized by Apple.

Multilingual typing should just work. Now it does.

Teebots is your little team of AI bots, running on your own computer. No server to set up, no account to create.
Make a few bots, each good at one thing: one gathers notes, one drafts the weekly report, one keeps an eye on a website. Put them in a group chat and @ the one you want. Each bot has its own folder, memory and browser logins, and the group shares a memory too, so you only say a preference once.

Add your own model key to start: Claude, OpenAI, DeepSeek, Kimi and more are built in, plus any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with fallback if the main model can't be reached. Requests go straight from your computer to the provider, not through us. Teebots collects no usage stats. Before submitting or paying, a bot stops and asks you.
Free for macOS (Apple silicon). Windows and Linux coming soon.

apps.name: HushNotes
apps.tagline: Floating Mac notes, hidden from screen shares
apps.description:
Notes that float on top of every app and stay out of your screen shares. Save text from any app with one hotkey. Native macOS, no account. $9.99, pay once.

HushNotes is a native Mac notes app that lives in your menu bar, so you never have to switch away from what you are doing to write something down.

The problem: you keep notes open during calls and demos, and sharing your screen means hiding them or risking the wrong window going out. Saving a line of text usually means switching apps too.

What it does

Save text from any app: select it and press Option + Shift + Space. It lands in your notes without leaving the app you are in.
Floating notes: keep a note above every window while you work.

People search for an alternative when the free app feels too small. They want a picture of the whole disk, or they want caches and old backups gone, or they already dragged an app to the Trash and the leftovers are still there. Those are three different jobs. A cleaner that deletes caches will not walk you through uninstalling Slack. An uninstaller will not tell you that an iPhone backup is the thing filling the drive.

If you still want to uninstall

Mole uninstalls an app and reviews the leftover files with it. It also maps disk usage and clears caches. The site listed $19 once, with a 14-day refund, and macOS 14 or later. That is the closest paid step up from AppCleaner on this shelf, because uninstalling is still in the product. See mole.fit.

Plumby is aimed at the leftovers and the bulky stuff: caches, macOS installers, old videos, iPhone backups, and files left after you dragged an app to the Trash. It removes only what you select, and personal files start unticked. The site listed $29 a year or $79 once, and macOS 15 or later. It is the wrong buy on an older Mac. Confirm the price on plumby.app.

If the disk is full, not the app

ByteSweep explains what is using the space and waits for you to approve a deletion. The developer says nothing is removed until you say so, and that anything cleaned can be put back for 7 days. The site listed $29.99 once for one computer, a 3-day trial on the Mac, and macOS 14 or later. It does not present itself as the thing you drag an app onto. Use it when the question is "what is this 40 GB," not "how do I remove this app." Read bytesweep.app.

The practical split is the screen. If you only use a notched MacBook, NotchDodo is the one whose site lists the music, calendar, files, and notes in one hover. If you also work on a display with no notch, Droppy is the one that says it still has a place to sit.

posts.excerpt: Screen Charm and ScreenToast zoom after you record. Boom skips the editing timeline. Better Shot is the free recorder already on this shelf.

Boom, if you do not want a timeline
Better Shot is already on this shelf

posts.html:
A Screen Studio alternative is a recorder that makes a demo look edited. Screen Charm and ScreenToast add the zoom after you stop. Boom never opens a timeline.

Screen Studio records the screen, the camera, and the audio, then animates zooms and smooths the cursor so a product demo does not look like a raw capture. Its site says new licenses are a subscription, and that the old one-time license is no longer sold to new buyers. A current dollar price was not on the homepage. Check screen.studio before you pay.

What Screen Studio is actually for

People looking for a Screen Studio alternative usually want the zoom, not a blank recording. The click should pull the frame in, and the cursor should stop jittering. If you only need a file of the screen with no effects, the built-in macOS recorder is enough, and so is a simpler app. If you need a phone in the shot, that is a different tool and it is not on this list.

Zoom after you record

Screen Charm records the full screen, one window, or an area, plus camera, microphone, and system audio. When the recording ends, it puts a zoom on each click. You can change the zoom or delete it. The site listed $99 once, with $149 shown as the regular price, and said there is no subscription. macOS 14 or later is recommended. Confirm the price on screencharm.com.

ScreenToast is the same kind of recorder, and it goes one step further: it can write a script from what you did on screen and read that script aloud. Zooms land on the clicks. The site listed Pro at $7 a month, or $59 for the year, and said you need Pro to export. It needs macOS 14 or later. See screentoast.com.

Between those two, the split is the voiceover and the bill. Screen Charm is a one-time purchase and leaves the narration to you. ScreenToast will draft the narration and then charge a subscription if you want the file out.

Boom, if you do not want a timeline

Boom records and also presents live, with layout changes and zoom while you are talking. The developer says there is no editing timeline. You trim, then export. It is aimed at calls such as Zoom and Meet as well as a recording. The site offers a free trial and did not list a price. It needs macOS 13 or later. Check boomvideo.app.

Pick Boom if the Screen Studio step you wanted to skip is the edit, not the zoom. Do not pick it if you wanted to adjust every click zoom after the fact. That control is what Screen Charm keeps.

Better Shot is already on this shelf

Better Shot is the free recorder from the CleanShot guide. It records the screen and the camera, and the developer says it can add auto-zoom, with no account and no watermark. It needs macOS 14 or later. It is the one to try before paying $99 or starting a subscription. It is not a dedicated demo studio, and this page is not a timed comparison against Screen Studio.

CleanShot X is the suite people mean when they say "screenshot app": capture, annotation, scrolling pages, screen recording, and a cloud link. On its pricing page, Basic was $35 once, with a year of updates and 1 GB of cloud, then an optional $19 a year. Pro was $10 per user a month, billed annually, with unlimited cloud. Read cleanshot.com/pricing before you pay. The apps below do not all replace that whole list.

What CleanShot X is actually for

If the missing piece is a still image of a window or a long page, you want a screenshot app. If the missing piece is a video of the screen, you want a recorder, and a still-image tool will feel incomplete. If the shots are already in a folder and you cannot find the one with the error message, you want search, not another capture hotkey.

Shottr, for the screenshot itself

Shottr captures an area, a window, or the full screen, and it can scroll a page or a chat and stitch that into one image. It also reads text and QR codes, measures distances on screen, and picks colors. The site says it runs on macOS 10.15 or later. It does not advertise screen recording.

You can download it free. The purchase page says that copy asks you to upgrade after 30 days. Basic is $12 once, for one person and up to five computers, and a license is required for commercial use. That is a one-time payment, not a subscription. Confirm it on shottr.cc.

Shottr is the closest swap when CleanShot's cloud and video editor are not the reason you opened it. You are paying, if you pay, for the still image and the measuring tools.

Better Shot takes the screenshot and the recording. You can mark up a still with arrows and text, and you can record the screen and the camera, then trim the video. The developer says the price is $0, with no account and no watermark, and calls the app open source. It needs macOS 14 or later, on Apple silicon or Intel. See bettershot.site.

This is the one to pick when you wanted CleanShot because it records, not only because it grabs a window. It will not run on a Mac stuck before Sonoma. Shottr will.

What Wispr Flow is actually for

People searching for a Wispr Flow alternative usually want to stop typing in email, chat, and notes. They do not want a separate window where they drop an audio file. If the recording already exists, that is a transcription app, and it is the last section of this guide.

  • Text should appear in the app you already have open

  • You would rather pay once than subscribe
  • You are transcribing a meeting file you already have: skip to MacWhisper

On the Mac: HoldSpeak and Precis

HoldSpeak uses a key you hold, then types into the Mac app under the cursor. The developer says recording and transcription stay on the device, that your voice is not uploaded, and that there is no account. It needs Apple silicon and macOS 14.6 or later. There is a 7-day trial, then a one-time payment. The site did not show a dollar amount when this was written. Read holdspeak.com before you pay.

Precis is the same kind of tool, with a tighter system requirement. The developer says speech recognition runs on the Mac, that no audio is sent to a server, and that the recording is deleted once the words are typed. The site listed a founding price of $19, then $29, paid once, and said the app needs macOS 26.5 on Apple silicon. Confirm both on myprecis.app.

That is useful for a meeting you already captured. It is not the same as holding a key in Mail and having the sentence appear. People mix the names up because both sit near "Whisper." posts.title: Best Logseq Alternative for Networked Notes (2026)
posts.excerpt: Anytype is the Logseq alternative for private, structured notes. Compare objects, encryption, and sync with Logseq's markdown outliner before you switch.

toc.label: When a Logseq alternative makes sense
Logseq and Anytype, side by side

posts.html:
Anytype is the Logseq alternative for people who want notes stored as objects, not only as an outline, The tagline mentions encryption. The description does not say how that encryption is set up.

Logseq is the better fit when the work is a daily outline in plain files. Anytype is the better fit when those notes need fields, links between types of things, and peer-to-peer sync. The description does not say the sync is encrypted by default. This page is a comparison, not a ranking of every notes app.

When a Logseq alternative makes sense

Logseq is already a strong outliner. People usually look past it for a specific gap, not because the outliner is broken. A switch is worth it if you need:

  • A note that has fields, such as author or status, instead of only bullets
  • Tagline mentions encryption. The description does not say it is on without a setup step
  • Sync between your own devices that does not depend on a folder you manage
  • Relations between notes, such as a book linked to a person
  • A layout that is closer to a database than to a journal

If none of those are the problem, Logseq does not need replacing.

What Logseq is for

Logseq is a free, open-source outliner. Notes live as Markdown or Org files on your Mac. Pages link to each other, and a graph is built from those links, often starting from a daily note. That file-based setup is the point: you can open the same text in another editor, and you can sync the folder with git or iCloud yourself. Official sync, if you want it, is a separate paid service.

It is a poor match if you wanted each note to be a record with typed fields. You can fake that with properties, but the app is still an outliner.

What Anytype changes

Anytype keeps notes on the device first, then syncs them peer-to-peer. A note can be an object with a type. A book can have an author field and a status, and that author can be its own object. The app is free to start. Paid plans add remote storage and sharing limits, so check current prices on anytype.io before you pay.

The desktop code is published under the Any Source Available License. That is not the same as Logseq's open-source license, so do not treat Anytype as a drop-in open-source project.

Logseq and Anytype, side by side

AnytypeLogseq

EncryptionTagline mentions encryption. Not described as on by defaultNot on unless you add it
SyncPeer-to-peer, includedYour own files, or paid Logseq Sync
Files you can open elsewhereExport, not the live formatMarkdown or Org on disk
LicenseSource-availableOpen source
PriceFree to start; storage plans are paidApp is free; official sync is paid
Best fitPrivate notes with structureDaily outline and a graph

Stay with Logseq if

  • You write in bullets and a daily journal
  • You want the notes as plain files in a folder
  • You already sync that folder with git or iCloud
  • You use the graph as the way you find old notes
  • You want an open-source app specifically

Switch to Anytype if

  • You want a book, a person, and a project to be different kinds of notes
  • You want those notes linked by a relation, not only by a wiki-style link
  • You want the app whose tagline mentions encryption
  • You want sync between devices without running your own folder sync
  • You are fine exporting if you later want plain Markdown

The difference that matters

The useful difference is the shape of a note. In Logseq, a reading log is a page of bullets: title, then author, then a quote. In Anytype, the same log can be a Book object with those as fields, and the author can be a Person object you reuse on the next book. If you will not use fields and relations, you are paying complexity for a feature you will not open.

posts.title: Best Ulysses Alternative for Writing (2026)
posts.excerpt: iA Writer is the Ulysses alternative for focused Markdown and a one-time Mac purchase. Compare the library and the subscription before you switch.

toc.label: When a Ulysses alternative makes sense
Ulysses and iA Writer, side by side

posts.html:
iA Writer is the Ulysses alternative for people who want a Markdown file and a quiet page, bought once on the Mac, instead of a writing library on a subscription.

Ulysses is the better fit when one library has to hold many projects, with goals and publishing built in. iA Writer is the better fit when the draft itself is the whole job. This page compares those two jobs. It does not claim one app is better at everything.

When a Ulysses alternative makes sense

Ulysses is a full writing app for Apple devices. People look for something else when the library, or the subscription, is the part they do not want. A switch is worth it if you need:

  • A page that gets out of the way of the sentence you are writing
  • A Markdown file in a folder, not only inside an app library
  • A Mac purchase you pay once, rather than a subscription
  • The same kind of editor on Windows, not only on Apple devices
  • Less organization around the draft

If you live in the library, sheets, and publishing tools, Ulysses is doing the job you bought it for.

What Ulysses is for

Ulysses is a Markdown writing suite for Mac, iPhone, and iPad. Projects sit in one library. You can set a writing goal, keep notes beside a draft, and publish from the app. Sync stays inside Apple's ecosystem. The app is sold as a subscription, so the cost continues after the first year. Check the developer's current price before you subscribe. This page does not quote it, because that number changes.

What iA Writer changes

iA Writer is a markdown editor built around a calm page and plain-text files. The Mac version is a separate purchase from the iPhone and iPad version, and from Windows. On the developer's buy page, the Mac app was listed at $49.99. Confirm that before you pay. A purchase covers the current version; major upgrades can cost extra later.

Stay with Ulysses if

  • You keep many articles or chapters in one library
  • You use writing goals and publishing from the same app
  • You work only on a Mac, iPhone, and iPad
  • You want sheets, keywords, and filters around the draft
  • A subscription is an acceptable way to pay for that library

Switch to iA Writer if

  • You want the current sentence highlighted and the rest dimmed
  • You want the draft as a Markdown file you can move
  • You also write on Windows
  • You would rather pay once per platform than subscribe
  • You do not need a built-in publishing pipeline

The difference that matters

The useful difference is where the draft lives. In Ulysses, a chapter is an item in the library, with a goal count beside it. In iA Writer, the listing says the Mac app is a markdown editor built around a calm page and plain-text files. It does not describe a focus mode that fades other sentences. If you will miss the library, iA Writer will feel empty. If the library was the part you were avoiding, that emptiness is the feature.
